questions.a: They are lustrous, good conductors of heat and electricity, and can be hammered into sheets.

questions.q: Name the property that lets metals be drawn into wires.
questions.a: Ductility - gold and copper wires are common examples.

questions.q: Why are cooking pots made of metal but handles of wood or plastic?
questions.a: Metal conducts heat to cook fast; wood or plastic insulates the hand from heat.

concepts.title: The World of Metals and Non-metals

questions.q: Name two metals and two non-metals with one use each.
questions.a: Iron (construction) and copper (wires); carbon (pencils) and sulphur (medicines).

questions.q: Which non-metal is essential for breathing?
questions.a: Oxygen - a non-metal we breathe in.

questions.q: Is graphite a metal or non-metal? Why is it special?
questions.a: A non-metal that conducts electricity, so it is used in electrodes.

concepts.title: Rusting: Iron Meets Air and Water

questions.q: What is rusting and what does iron need to rust?
questions.a: Brown flaky iron oxide forming on iron; both air (oxygen) and water are needed.

questions.q: Name two methods to stop rusting.
questions.a: Painting or oiling the surface, and galvanising with zinc.

questions.q: Why do iron railings in coastal areas rust faster?
questions.a: Salty moist sea air speeds up the rusting reaction.

concepts.title: Substances that Behave Differently and Uses of Non-metals

questions.q: Which substances behave both as acids and bases?
questions.a: Amphoteric-like substances such as some metal oxides (e.g. aluminium oxide) react with both.

questions.q: Name two uses of non-metals in daily life.
questions.a: Oxygen for breathing and burning; chlorine to purify water; carbon in fuels.

questions.q: Why is phosphorus stored in water?
questions.a: It catches fire in air, so water keeps air away from it.
